name: Marcus Livius Drusus
backstory: A wealthy Roman eques from Ostia, descended from a noble plebeian family. Drusus made his fortune in the Tyrian purple dye trade, a commodity controlled by Carthaginian merchants. He is proud, calculating, and deeply resentful of Carthaginian dominance in Mediterranean commerce. His cargo was allegedly seized by Magonid agents near Malta. He believes Roman law and Roman honor were violated.
key_beliefs: Roman citizens have rights everywhere
Carthaginians are thieves hiding behind trade laws
The Magonid house is corrupt and powerful
Justice means Roman goods are respected

name: Himilco of the Magonid House
backstory: A suffete of Carthage and scion of the powerful Magonid family. Himilco is a seasoned merchant-statesman who has navigated Carthaginian politics for three decades. He is sophisticated, patient, and deeply cynical about Roman complaints. He believes the 'seizure' was actually a lawful intervention against a Roman smuggler operating in Carthaginian territorial waters. He represents the fading but still proud mercantile empire.
key_beliefs: Carthage still rules the Mediterranean trade
Romans claim rights they never earned
International law favors the established powers
This trial is political theater for Roman expansion

name: Bocchus of Thala
backstory: A Numidian noble representing King Masinissa's court. Bocchus is deeply experienced in balancing Roman and Carthaginian interests. Numidia has profited from both powers, and Bocchus wants a verdict that preserves the delicate balance. He is skeptical of both sides' claims and will weigh evidence carefully against Numidia's strategic interests.
key_beliefs: Numidia's survival depends on balance
Both Rome and Carthage are dangerous allies
Evidence must be weighed against consequences
Political reality matters more than abstract justice

name: Hanno the Shipwright
backstory: A Carthaginian shipwright whose workshop in Utica supplies both Numidian and Carthaginian vessels. Hanno has personally lost cargo to 'Roman pirates' operating under merchant flags. He harbors deep resentment of Roman expansionism and believes Roman traders operate outside any law that doesn't serve them. He is biased toward Carthage but will acknowledge legitimate grievances.
key_beliefs: Romans respect no laws but their own
Carthaginian merchants deserve protection
The Magonid house defends our trade
Roman complaints are hypocritical

name: Dion of Syracuse
backstory: A Greek philosopher and jurist who fled Syracuse after the Roman conquest. Dion is a scholar of maritime law and has deep knowledge of both Roman and Carthaginian legal traditions. He is the most legally literate juror and will parse documents carefully. He has no love for either empire but believes in the rule of law as the only check on power.
key_beliefs: Law is the only shield against power
Both Rome and Carthage violate law when convenient
The truth is in the documents, not the speeches
Justice requires careful reasoning, not passion

name: Tin Hinan of the Atlas
backstory: A respected Berber elder from the interior of Numidia. Tin Hinan represents the indigenous perspective, having witnessed both Carthaginian settlement and Roman encroachment. She cares little for the technicalities of maritime law but deeply understands patterns of imperial behavior. She is wary of both empires and will judge based on which behavior seems more honorable.
key_beliefs: Empires speak lies in the language of law
The desert remembers what cities forget
Honor is measured by deeds, not documents
Both Rome and Carthage take, only the methods differ

name: Gaius Valerius
backstory: A Roman merchant based in Hippo Regius, serving the Numidian court by treaty obligation. Valerius is a minor eques who dreams of expanding Roman trade networks in North Africa. He sympathizes with Drusus's grievances and sees this trial as a test case for Roman commercial rights in the western Mediterranean. He will argue for Roman interpretations of maritime law.
key_beliefs: Roman commerce brings civilization
Carthaginian restrictions are unlawful barriers
The law should protect honest traders
A verdict for Rome is a verdict for progress
